transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
There's still no definitive word on the condition of the death row inmate who survived an execution
last night in Tennessee.
Christa Gail Pike was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder.
She was given two injections of lethal doses of a sedative, but she survived and was taken
to a nearby hospital.
Katherine Sweeney of Member Station WPLN spoke to NPR's "Here and Now" about the debate
surrounding executions, which in the wake of this latest development, Tennessee Governor
Bill Lee has put on hold in the state.
A lot of doctors here say basically only unethical doctors would sign up to be involved in this,
only unethical healthcare workers would, because every ethics code says they're not supposed
to participate in executions.
And so all we know is it was catastrophically wrong.
It was an enormous dose of a sedative and she was still breathing.
But we don't know much about her condition now, either.
They're being very secretive about it.
We do know that she is still alive, but that's about it.
A New York prosecutor now says he did not have access to full transcripts of a woman's
account of being raped at Cornell University in 2024 when he decided not to pursue the
case.
District Attorney Matthew Van Houten says he stopped the investigation after only reviewing
the woman's signed statement.
Here's NPR's Brian Mann.
Van Houten has said the former student, who alleged in a recent civil lawsuit that she
was gang-raped by seven male students, gave a different account to campus police two years
ago describing her participation in drug use and sex at a frat party as "voluntary, conscious,
and consensual."
But now more full transcripts of the woman's interviews with campus police investigators
have been reported by multiple news outlets.
They show she described the incident at the time in graphic terms as rape.
In a statement to WSKG Radio, Van Houten says he didn't see that information before stopping
the investigation.
"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to
police," Van Houten said.
Brian Mann, NPR News, Ithaca, New York.
Starting today, states will pay for a larger share of the bill to run the food assistance
program known as SNAP.
Here's NPR's Julianna Kim.
Last year's massive Republican tax and spending law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act,
included major changes to how SNAP is funded, shifting more of the costs onto states rather
than the federal government.
As a result, states may need to spend two to three times more in the future in order
to keep the food assistance program running.
That's according to the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality.
The key question now is how states will afford these new costs to SNAP.
Policy experts say states may need to raise taxes, cut funding for other programs, or
reduce access to food benefits.
When it comes as SNAP participation is already rapidly dropping.
Julianna Kim, NPR News.
Again, federal funding for costs including state SNAP workers will shrink by half.
It's NPR News.
A judge has ruled that the federal government cannot revive its reflecting pool vandalism
case against a former Olympic canoist, NPR's Rachel Treisman has details.
In a 26-page ruling, a DC Superior Court judge granted David Hearn's request to have his
reflecting pool case dismissed with prejudice, so it cannot be brought again.
The judge said that would have been a possibility because of the "political pressure brought
by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers."
Federal prosecutors dropped the vandalism charges against the former Olympic canoist
and three other people in late July, admitting that the reflecting pool damage was the result
of "botched installation."
President Trump continued to blame vandalism and lash out at prosecutors for saying otherwise,
prompting Hearn's legal fight to close the case for good.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
British counterterrorism police say they arrested a 27-year-old man in London today in connection
with a suspected terrorism plot on an airbase in England that's used by the US military.
Authorities say the suspect is a dual UK-Iranian national.
Five other men arrested Sunday were released on bail.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government sees "strong indications Iran played a role,"
a claim the Iranian embassy has denied.
The Russian government's threatening to stop supplying diesel to global energy markets
until sanctions against it are lifted.
President Vladimir Putin informed a think-tank forum in Moscow of his plans today, citing
losses from Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries.
President Trump's blamed those attacks for the economic hit to global delivery networks
that depend on diesel.
It's NPR.

topics.text: Death row inmate Christa Gail Pike survives execution in Tennessee, condition unknown
New York prosecutor says he lacked full transcripts in Cornell University rape case decision
States to pay larger share of SNAP food assistance program costs starting today
Judge dismisses reflecting pool vandalism case against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn
British counterterrorism police arrest 27-year-old man in connection with suspected airbase terrorism plot
Russian government threatens to halt diesel supplies until international sanctions are lifted
